newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: 124 sign nuclear test ban treaty; Fiji ratifies.
newsitem.headline: 124 sign nuclear test ban treaty; Fiji ratifies.

text.p: A total of 124 states have signed the nuclear test ban treaty over the past three weeks and Fiji has become the first to ratify the pact, the United Nations said on Monday.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, followed by the other declared nuclear powers -- Russia, France, Britain and China -- opened the signing ceremonies on Sept. 24 for the treaty to end all nuclear explosions.

It requires 44 nations with nuclear power to sign and then ratify it through their national legislatures before it comes into force. India, whose approval is necessary, has vowed never to sign "this unequal treaty" until the atomic powers devise a timetable for destroying their nuclear arsenals.

So far, 39 of the necessary 44 states have submitted signatures to the treaty at U.N. headquarters, with Egypt's ambassador, Nabil Elaraby, signing for his country on Monday. The five remaining states are Algeria, Bangladesh, North Korea along with India and Pakistan, which has said it would not agree to the pact until India does.

The 39 who have signed, excluding the five declared nuclear powers, are Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Egypt, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Netherlands, Norway, Peru, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, South Korea, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, Ukraine, Vietnam and Zaire.

Fiji is the only state to have ratified the treaty and deposited papers to this effect with U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, his spokeswoman, Sylvana Foa, said. But Clinton has said signature of the pact was tantamount to a ban on testing "even before the treaty formally enters into force."

Many of the signatures came from foreign ministers who were attending the U.N. General Assemby debate, which ended last Thursday. The treaty requires a conference in three to four years for members to decide how to accelerate the ratification process should India and others still refuse to join the pact.
Currently, the United States and Russia each deploy more than 7,000 warheads, France 512, Britain 464 and China 284.
The new treaty bans all explosions, including underground blasts. A 1963 treaty barred explosions in the atmosphere and another one in 1974 set a size limit on underground tests.

All five declared nuclear weapons states have imposed voluntary moratoriums on testing. The United States, Russia and Britain stopped testing between 1990 and 1992, while France and China ended blasts several months ago.
